performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The Requiem ends with a welcome: may angels lead you into paradise. Sopranos sing above the organ’s quick broken chords, with muted strings and, later, a harp.

sections.label: A · Sopranos over the organ’s broken chords
B · More voices gather on Jerusalem
C · Harp beneath the choir of angels
sections.mNote: The sopranos begin again over organ, harp and muted strings

sections.label: D · The sopranos sing of Lazarus
E · The choir’s final requiem
sections.mNote: All voices gather quietly on the word for rest

cues.title: The organ keeps shining
cues.text: The organ turns over quick broken chords in D major. Muted strings hold long notes above it, and the sopranos begin a rising line. There are no brass or woodwinds in this final movement.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 114–128: organ figuration, muted strings and empty wind and brass staves. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Voices gather on Jerusalem
cues.text: The divided tenors and basses join the sopranos on “Jerusalem”, entering pianissimo and growing together. The organ keeps its broken chords running beneath the longer choral notes.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 119–120: divided tenor and bass entries, pp and crescendo, over continuing organ figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A harp for the angels
cues.text: The harp adds rising semiquavers to the organ’s movement. Above them the sopranos sing “Chorus angelorum te suscipiat” — may the choir of angels receive you — marked dolce. The strings remain muted.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 121–123: harp entry and the soprano Chorus angelorum phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the Madeleine
cues.text: In 1924 the Requiem returns to the Madeleine for Fauré’s own state funeral. The church where he spent years as choirmaster and organist hears the work in its full orchestral version.
cues.evidence: The 1924 funeral and orchestral version: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9). National funeral and Madeleine appointments: https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/composer/gabriel-faure/biography; the funeral venue is also recorded in the site’s Fauré biography.

cues.title: The last word is rest
cues.text: The other voices join the sopranos on “requiem”, pianissimo. Organ and harp continue beneath them as the harmony settles into D major. The last choral chord is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 125–128: quiet choral entries on requiem, D major and the final fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lullaby of death
cues.text: Someone, Fauré told the interviewer Louis Aguettant in 1902, had called his Requiem “a lullaby of death”. That is how he felt death, he said: “a happy deliverance, an aspiration towards happiness beyond”.
cues.evidence: Fauré to Louis Aguettant, 12 July 1902, published in Comœdia, 1954, p. 6: “quelqu’un l’a appelé une berceuse de la mort. Mais c’est ainsi que je sens la mort: comme une délivrance heureuse, une aspiration au bonheur d’au-delà”. French text at http://www.rene-gagnaux.ch/inghelbrecht_desire-emile/faure_requiem.html. Translation ours.

transitions.title: The sopranos acquire a choir
transitions.from: A · Sopranos over the organ’s broken chords
transitions.to: B · More voices gather on Jerusalem
transitions.how: Divided tenors and basses enter on “Jerusalem”, pianissimo, beneath the sopranos. Double basses join the low strings. The voices crescendo together while the organ continues its quick broken chords, unchanged in pace.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 119–120: divided male voices, double-bass entry and crescendo.

transitions.title: A harp joins the organ
transitions.from: B · More voices gather on Jerusalem
transitions.to: C · Harp beneath the choir of angels
transitions.how: “Jerusalem” subsides, and the lower voices rest. The muted strings settle quietly as the harp begins rising semiquavers beside the organ’s running figure. The sopranos start “Chorus angelorum”, marked dolce.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 120–122: the end of Jerusalem, harp entry and soprano Chorus angelorum.

transitions.title: Lazarus in the soprano line
transitions.from: C · Harp beneath the choir of angels
transitions.to: D · The sopranos sing of Lazarus
transitions.how: The sopranos continue with “Et cum Lazaro quondam paupere” — and with Lazarus, once a poor man. Organ and harp maintain their broken chords while the muted strings crescendo. The vocal line climbs towards “aeternam”, eternal.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 123–125, rehearsals D–E: the Lazarus text and the ascent to aeternam.

transitions.title: The choir settles into D major
transitions.from: D · The sopranos sing of Lazarus
transitions.how: The soprano line descends from “aeternam” towards “requiem”. The remaining voices join quietly, and the strings drop to pianissimo. Organ and harp carry on beneath the sustained choir as the harmony finds D major and the final word is prolonged.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 125–128: quiet choral entry, sustained strings and closing D major.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: VII. In paradisum, printed pp. 114–128: muted strings and organ, divided voices at Jerusalem, and the harp’s entry at Chorus angelorum.

timeline.note: Organ semiquavers shimmer beneath the sopranos. The strings play with mutes.
Divided tenors and basses sing “Jerusalem”; the double basses enter pianissimo.
The harp enters with rising semiquavers under “Chorus angelorum”. The double basses rest.
The double basses return as the choir grows towards its final prayer for rest.
The voices sing “requiem” in turn, pianissimo. Strings hold long notes; organ and harp keep moving.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.27 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 3 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.44 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: He spent his days at the organ and in the classroom, saving for songs and chamber music the harmonies nobody else could quite imagine.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
The boy kept slipping into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and the little instrument in its chapel gave Gabriel Fauré his first musical happiness. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he lived among plainchant, organ exercises and the interweaving voices of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was done, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers far outside their syllabus. Fauré acquired a teacher, a champion and a friend who would stay beside him for sixty years. He left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine: a French prayer unfolding over a flowing keyboard part, each new choral entry joining a phrase already under way.
